doc.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

chapter: Feel, skank and the New Orleans way
title: Playing behind the beat and New Orleans' ancestral resonance
summary: Why musicians move to New Orleans and how one learns to play behind the beat naturally, by playing with people who do it.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well you just said playing a little sloppy without being pretentious. And I can see how that would be difficult for a musician who might say, “I want to move to New Orleans and get in the music scene.”
A lot of people do that, because it’s the last place left that has ancestral resonance in the music that’s being played today.

You know I mean you play at Preservation Hall and the bass player is putting his peg in the hole that’s been worn in the wood that’s been there since the seventeen hundreds that other bass players have put untold hours of energy and so it’s hard not to feel what came before. And that’s leaving us in New Orleans, but it’s still there as opposed to most everywhere else.
But feeling — how do I say this? Consciously trying to play behind the beat is hard. It has to come natural, right? And how do you make it natural?
You play with people that do it naturally, and you understand, oh man, I’m really comfortable here. And then it becomes part of your vocabulary.
